column1: # topic: Chapter 2: Old Worlds, New Worlds

column2: Ming China was the wealthiest power of the fifteenth-century world, and its prized silks, porcelain, and other goods anchored the trade of all Eurasia.
Zheng He commanded China's enormous treasure fleet on voyages that reached as far as eastern Africa before Ming rulers ended long-distance expeditions.
The Ottoman Empire was a powerful Islamic state that controlled the trade routes between Asia and Europe and alarmed Christian Europe with its conquests.
Mehmet II was the Ottoman sultan who conquered Constantinople, seizing a great Christian city and the trading hub between Europe and Asia.
Prince Henry the Navigator of Portugal sponsored voyages down the African coast and improvements in ships and navigation that launched Portugal's overseas expansion.
The Portuguese pioneered Atlantic exploration by colonizing the Wine Islands, building slave-worked sugar plantations, trading along West Africa, and opening a sea route to India.
The Wine Islands, the volcanic-soil Atlantic island groups of the Canaries, Madeira, and the Azores, were where Portugal spread slave-run sugar plantations after earlier Mediterranean plantations.
The West African kingdoms were organized states with enough military power to force Portuguese traders to negotiate with their rulers as relative equals.
Bartolomeu Dias was the Portuguese navigator who rounded the Cape of Good Hope at Africa's southern tip, proving that ships could reach the Indian Ocean.
Vasco da Gama was the Portuguese navigator who sailed around Africa to India, opening Portugal's direct sea trade with Asia.
Christopher Columbus, a mariner from Genoa, persuaded Spain to fund a westward voyage to Asia and instead reached the Caribbean, which he wrongly believed lay near the Indies.
Ferdinand and Isabella were the monarchs of Spain who completed the reconquista, funded Columbus's voyage, and built a powerful centralized kingdom.
Amerigo Vespucci was a Florentine navigator who recognized that the lands Columbus reached were a New World, and America was named after him.
John Cabot was an Italian mariner sailing for England who searched for a northwest passage to Asia and reached North America near Newfoundland, giving England its claim.
The Taino were the Caribbean islanders Columbus first met and mislabeled Indians, and Spanish warfare, forced labor, hunger, and disease nearly destroyed them.
Bartolomé de Las Casas was a Dominican friar who renounced conquest and condemned Spanish cruelty toward Indians, and his writings fueled the Black Legend.
The Aztecs ruled an unpopular Mexican tribute empire whose resentful subject peoples joined Cortés and whose population was devastated by smallpox.
Hernán Cortés was the Spanish conquistador who allied with the Aztecs' Indian enemies, captured Tenochtitlán, and destroyed the Aztec Empire.
Moctezuma was the Aztec emperor who welcomed Cortés into Tenochtitlán as a guest, only to be taken captive when the Spaniards turned hospitality into domination.
Francisco Pizarro was the Spanish conquistador who, with his brothers, had conquered the Inca Empire by 1532 using political divisions, disease, technology, and luck.
The Inca Empire was the powerful Andean state of South America that fell to Pizarro after internal divisions, smallpox, and Spanish weapons weakened it.
Juan Ponce de León, the Spanish conqueror of Puerto Rico, made the first official Spanish mainland expedition, named Florida, and was mortally wounded by Calusa Indians in 1521.
Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca survived a failed Florida expedition and wandered for years across Texas and northern Mexico, and his reports of Indian societies spurred later Spanish expeditions.
Esteban was an enslaved African who survived with Cabeza de Vaca, completing the extraordinary trek across Texas and northern Mexico.
Hernando de Soto was a Spanish conquistador who ravaged the chiefdoms of the Southeast while searching unsuccessfully for North American gold.
Francisco Vázquez de Coronado, aged 29, led 300 Spaniards and 1,000 Mexican Indian warriors into the Southwest in 1539 seeking rich cities but found only mud-and-straw pueblos.
Martin Luther was a German monk who attacked the sale of indulgences, taught justification by faith alone, and made the Bible the sole religious authority.
John Calvin was a French theologian in Geneva who taught predestination and the calling and urged Christians to remake society according to God's law.
The Huguenots were French Calvinists who, facing persecution at home, founded Fort Caroline in Florida until Spain destroyed it.
The Puritans were English Calvinists who demanded that the Church of England purify itself by removing bishops, elaborate ceremonies, and other Catholic practices.
Pedro Menéndez de Avilés was the Spanish commander who founded St. Augustine and wiped out the French Huguenot settlement at Fort Caroline.
Henry VIII was the English king who broke with the pope after being denied an annulment and made himself head of the Church of England.
Elizabeth I was England's Protestant queen who, fearing Spain, challenged Spanish power and licensed private ventures to colonize America.
Humphrey Gilbert was an English soldier who received England's first charter to colonize America but was lost at sea before founding a settlement.
Walter Raleigh was an English courtier who received a royal patent, named the land Virginia, and sponsored the Roanoke colonies.
Richard Hakluyt the younger was an English clergyman who promoted colonization as a source of commodities, markets, Protestant influence, and strength against Spain.
Wingina was the Roanoke weroance who welcomed the English to gain trade goods and weapons but was murdered after English brutality turned his people against them.
John White was the English artist and governor of the second Roanoke colony who hoped for peace with the Indians and later found the colony vanished.
James I was the Stuart king of England who imprisoned Walter Raleigh and favored orderly, Crown-supervised colonies over independent adventurers.
Bernal Díaz was a lieutenant of Cortés whose memoir, written decades later, describes the Spaniards' wonder at Tenochtitlán's great marketplace.
Bernardino de Sahagún was a Spanish missionary who recorded Aztec informants' memories of their society and of the conquest, preserving the Indian side of the story.
Hispaniola, the Caribbean island now shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic, held the first Spanish settlements in the Americas and became Spain's base for conquering the Caribbean.
Upper Guinea and Lower Guinea were the coastal regions of West Africa, Upper Guinea stretching south from the Senegal River and Lower Guinea running east along the Gulf of Guinea.
Giovanni Caboto, backed by Henry VII, sailed from Bristol in spring 1497, reported a new-found island rich in cod and mast trees, and earned a £10 reward.
Hy-Brasil, the mythical Isle of the Blessed, was the island English mariners searched for west of Ireland in the 1480s and 1490s.
St. John's, Newfoundland, was the informal hub of the North Atlantic fishery, where crews gathered supplies, traded with Native people, and departed each autumn.
Constantinople, now Istanbul, was the Christian city bridging Europe and Asia and a premier trading hub until Ottoman Sultan Mehmet II conquered it in 1453.
Saladin was the Muslim leader who reconquered Jerusalem in the twelfth century, pushing European investors to move sugar plantations to eastern Mediterranean islands.
San Salvador was Columbus's name for the Bahamas bay where the Niña, Pinta, and Santa Maria anchored on October 12, 1492, which Columbus mistook for land near Japan.
Tenochtitlán, the Aztec capital of roughly 250,000 people, fell to Cortés's siege in August 1521 and became Mexico City, headquarters of Spanish bureaucracy.
Doña Marina was the Native woman who translated for Cortés during his first meetings with Moctezuma's representatives in 1519.
Potosí was the Andean silver-mining city whose 120,000 people by 1570 made it larger than any city in Spain or its American empire.
The Calusa were the Florida Indians who, knowing Spaniards as slave raiders, resisted Juan Ponce de León and mortally wounded him in 1521.
Pánfilo de Narváez led 300 men into Florida in 1528, ignored Cabeza de Vaca's warning, separated from his force near Tampa Bay, and disappeared.
The Turk was the Indian guide who led Coronado onto the Great Plains toward Quivira, and Coronado had the Turk strangled in present-day Kansas.
The declining Mississippian chiefdoms of the Southeast were seen by Europeans only on de Soto's expedition, which hastened their shift to decentralized confederacies.

column1: Giovanni da Verrazzano and Jacques Cartier
column2: Giovanni da Verrazzano explored North America's eastern coast in 1524, and Jacques Cartier explored the St. Lawrence River valley in 1534, 1535, and 1541.
Jean Ribault led 150 Norman Huguenots to Parris Island in 1562 and a larger group to found Fort Caroline in 1564, before Menéndez killed Ribault.
Fort Caroline was the 1564 French Huguenot settlement south of present-day Jacksonville, allied with the Timucua, that Menéndez destroyed in 1565.
The Timucua were the Florida Indians who allied with the French Huguenots at Fort Caroline in 1564.
Sir Richard Grenville and Ralph Lane alienated the Roanoke people by burning a village and corn stores over a stolen cup, and Lane's men killed Wingina.
Thomas Hariot studied Roanoke's resources, and Hariot's 1588 report, with John White's drawings of Native people, became a major source on coastal Algonquians.
Croatoan was the island near Cape Hatteras whose name John White found carved on a post at the empty Roanoke fort in 1590.
Simon Ferdinando was the pilot who in July 1587 left Raleigh's second colony at Roanoke Island rather than Chesapeake Bay.

column1: Michel de Montaigne and André Thevet
column2: Michel de Montaigne mocked European assumptions that Indians lacked trade, letters, and laws, while André Thevet, visiting Brazil in 1557, read Native nakedness as lust.

column1: Catherine of Aragon and Anne Boleyn
column2: Henry VIII's wife Catherine of Aragon bore Mary but no son, and after the pope refused an annulment Henry married Anne Boleyn.
Edward VI's six-year reign helped English Protestants, while Catholic Mary became queen in 1553 and persecuted them until Elizabeth I succeeded in 1558.
